narrate.summary: Reliability analysis of a phased mission system is complicated because the system structure changes between phases, and component survival links the phases. The paper develops a survival-signature method that separates system structure from component lifetime distributions and handles different component types appearing in different phases. It derives reliability calculations for general lifetime distributions, subject to its component-type and dependence assumptions, and describes a simpler treatment for exponential lifetimes. The authors illustrate the method with three numerical examples, including a space mission, using specified component lifetime distributions and failure rates rather than field observations. The calculated results agree with independent methods reported in the literature, and the examples show that reliability can drop suddenly when a phase change makes earlier non-critical component failures critical.
narrate.key_results: For the first example, reported system reliability is 0.99501 at 30 hours, and the results agree with an independent method cited by the authors. In the Weibull example, the phase boundary at 10 hours produces a reliability jump of about 2.3 × 10^-4; the reported reliability at 200 hours is 0.998910. In the space-mission example, reported reliability at 45864 hours is 0.98943, again in agreement with an independent method. These are numerical illustrations, not estimates from observed lifetime data.

narrate.summary: This paper develops a parametric model for step-stress time-to-event data when some individuals or items may be immune to the applied stress. It addresses the limitation of the cumulative exposure model, which can imply an abrupt hazard change when stress changes, by using a continuous hazard transition with a lag before the new stress takes effect. The susceptible lifetimes can follow Weibull, linear failure rate, or generalized exponential distributions, while a logistic model links covariates to the probability of being cured. The authors estimate model parameters with an expectation-maximization algorithm and evaluate the approach using an altitude decompression sickness study of 40 subjects and simulated data. In the study data, the Weibull model fit best, with an estimated lag of 110 minutes and a cured fraction of about 18 percent.
narrate.key_results: For the 40-subject altitude study, the Weibull model had the highest maximized log-likelihood, -38.7093, and the smallest reported Kolmogorov-Smirnov distance, 0.0502; the corresponding values for the linear failure rate model were -41.1311 and 0.0949, and for the generalized exponential model were -39.6485 and 0.0589. The estimated stress-effect lag was 110 minutes, and the Weibull model estimated that 18 percent of the population was cured; the test for a cured fraction had a reported p-value of 0.0019. The covariates were significant in the reported test, with a p-value of 0.002; increasing body fat or age was associated with a lower probability of immunity, while increasing maximal oxygen uptake was associated with a higher probability. In simulations with sample sizes of 40, 80, 120, 160, and 200, 1,000 replications, and 20 percent censored observations, parameter bias and mean squared error decreased as sample size increased, and the algorithm stopped within 35 iterations in all reported cases.

narrate.summary: The paper estimates component lifetime distributions when a repairable system has multiple identical sockets but the socket responsible for each replacement is unknown. In the cylinder dataset, the lognormal model was selected by both the frequentist and Bayesian selection procedures. The estimated mean component lifetime was 11.0519 years by the Bayesian method and 10.9345 years by the expectation-maximization method, with similar estimated reliability curves.

narrate.summary: This review describes the Birnbaum-Saunders lifetime distribution, developed to model fatigue failure caused by repeated cyclic stress. It covers the model’s lifetime interpretation, distribution properties, parameter estimation, censoring methods, regression, and multivariate and generalized extensions. The distribution has a unimodal hazard function, so its failure rate can rise and then fall rather than remain monotone. The authors illustrate methods using fatigue tests on aluminum coupons and ball bearings, as well as insurance and bone-mineral data. Their central conclusion is that the distribution has a useful physical basis and a broad set of extensions and inference methods, while many research questions remain open.
narrate.key_results: The review reports that the hazard function of the standard model is always unimodal and that its long-term behavior approaches a constant. For 101 aluminum-coupon fatigue observations, the reported ML estimates were alpha 0.170385 and beta 131.818792. For the insurance example, the fitted model’s KS distance was 0.1385 with a p-value of 0.6130, which the authors considered a good fit. For a progressively censored ball-bearing example, the EM procedure converged in 24 to 44 iterations across the three censoring schemes; the estimated shape parameters ranged from 0.1484 to 0.1639 and scale estimates from 194.0795 to 195.8228 hours.

narrate.summary: This introductory review describes reliability methods for polymeric materials, which can lose functional properties after long exposure to environmental conditions or repeated stress. It covers degradation measured repeatedly without destroying the sample, degradation measured by destructive tests, and fatigue testing of polymer composites. narrate.summary: The paper compares placing redundant components beside individual components with placing redundancy around an entire k-out-of-n system. It studies both active redundancy, where components operate simultaneously, and cold redundancy, where a spare begins operating after a failure. The authors model the component and redundancy lifetimes as independent random variables, while allowing component lifetimes to differ. Their theoretical results favor component-level redundancy for systems requiring more than one functioning component.

The proofs state that the probability that the system-level allocation outlasts the component-level allocation is zero, while the reverse comparison has positive probability for k from 2 through n. These are theoretical comparisons; the paper reports no numerical estimates or data-based validation.

narrate.summary: The paper addresses early identification of equipment that is degrading or likely to have a shorter-than-usual life, rather than estimating a continuous remaining useful life. For comparison, the strongest non-TTC results in those Duffing conditions were 0.752, 0.839, 0.987, 0.999, and 0.999, respectively. In the early-detection experiment on C-MAPSS dataset 4, the authors report that TTC accuracy is significantly better in the initial stages, while some baselines approach comparable accuracy only after more cycles have been observed; no numerical lead time is reported.

narrate.summary: Estimating small structural failure probabilities with direct simulation can require very large numbers of costly model evaluations, while standard polynomial chaos expansions can be inaccurate in the response tails and do not provide local error estimates. Its active method is tested using simulated model outputs for a four-branch series-system benchmark, a two-dimensional truss, and a structural frame. The results show estimates comparable to reference simulations and to active Kriging, using substantially fewer evaluations than direct simulation in the examples. The frame case also shows that the method can provide useful uncertainty bounds when the competing active Kriging analysis does not converge within its evaluation budget.
narrate.key_results: For the four-branch benchmark, A-bPCE estimated failure probability as 4.62 × 10^-3, compared with the reference 4.46 × 10^-3, using 167 model evaluations; active learning reliability analysis using Kriging and Monte Carlo simulation estimated 4.52 × 10^-3 using 200 evaluations, while the reference used 10^8 samples. For the structural frame, A-bPCE estimated 1.49 × 10^-3 with reported bounds of 1.42 × 10^-3 to 1.62 × 10^-3 using 235 evaluations, compared with an importance-sampling reference estimate of 1.54 × 10^-3 and bounds of 1.51 × 10^-3 to 1.56 × 10^-3. For cause 2 under the same setting, the mean squared error was 0.482; the exact interval was unavailable in 25 replications, while exact and bootstrap interval coverage was 96% and 95%. narrate.summary: This paper introduces a new joint progressive censoring (NJPC) scheme for comparing lifetimes from two populations in a life test. In the reported comparisons, the new scheme often has lower estimation error than the existing scheme, and bootstrap confidence intervals are shorter while giving coverage near their target level.

In a reported 90% confidence interval (CI) comparison, the bootstrap interval for the first population had average length 1.279 and coverage 91.80%, while the exact interval had average length 2.920 and coverage 89.80%. The authors report that the simulated CIs generally had coverage close to the nominal level and that bootstrap intervals were shorter in the cases shown. For one analysis of the airplane data under the first censoring scheme, the estimated mean lifetimes were 59.4 and 114.0 hours.

narrate.summary: This paper studies how to estimate rare failure probabilities when engineering simulations are expensive and have many uncertain inputs. The authors model the simulation response with a canonical low-rank approximation (LRA), built from sums of products of univariate polynomial functions, and compare it with sparse polynomial chaos expansions (PCE). They test the methods on four simulated examples: a beam, a truss, a heat-conduction model with a spatially varying coefficient, and a frame, with input dimensions from 5 to 53. The surrogate models are built from relatively small experimental designs and then sampled computationally to estimate response distributions and failure probabilities. Across these examples, LRA generally estimates extreme response probabilities more accurately than sparse PCE when the experimental design is small relative to the input dimension, while also providing a broader probabilistic description of the response.
narrate.key_results: For the beam example, with 30 original-model evaluations, LRA estimated a reliability index of 4.32 for the largest threshold, compared with the analytical value of 4.25, a relative error smaller than 2%; sparse PCE did not estimate the corresponding failure probability at that design size. For the truss, with 50 evaluations, LRA estimated failure probabilities down to 4.73 × 10^-6, against an importance-sampling reference of 3.90 × 10^-6, and its reliability-index differences from reference were no more than 3%. For the heat-conduction model, LRA with 500 evaluations gave failure probabilities of 3.22 × 10^-4 and 7.35 × 10^-5 for the two highest temperature thresholds studied; the authors could not afford reference evaluations of the original model at those thresholds. For the frame, LRA’s reliability-index error stayed below 5% with 500 evaluations and below 4% with 1,000, while sparse PCE errors at the largest threshold exceeded 10% and 5%, respectively. The authors also report that the number of unknowns in LRA grows linearly with input dimension, unlike the full polynomial expansion, and that the surrogate can be reused for different thresholds without further evaluations of the original model.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors do not identify a specific technical limitation of their method. They state that further studies are needed to establish its efficacy across diverse reliability applications and note that tensor formats beyond the canonical form are an active research topic.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The evidence comes from four simulated examples, including finite-element models, rather than field measurements or operational failure data, so performance in real infrastructure settings is not established. For the most extreme heat-conduction thresholds, the original model was too costly to provide a reference result, so the reported surrogate estimates there could not be independently checked against that model. narrate.future_work_stated: The authors propose studying the method in more diverse reliability applications and investigating its ability to predict extreme responses in high-dimensional models. They also identify tensor approximation formats beyond the canonical formulation as a direction for further investigation.
narrate.future_work_unstated: Evaluate the approach with measured infrastructure data and quantify how uncertainty in input distributions and dependence assumptions affects rare-event estimates. Further work could also test additional failure mechanisms and system-level failure criteria, and develop decision-focused methods that use the surrogate estimates to compare risk-reduction or inspection choices.

narrate.summary: Random failure events make the Net Present Value (NPV) of a maintenance strategy uncertain, while repeatedly running the VME simulator across all possible strategies is computationally expensive. The paper models the simulator’s full NPV distribution by emulating its quantile functions, representing them with selected basis functions and Gaussian process metamodels. It tests the approach on a toy simulator and on simulated maintenance decisions for four identical systems at different power plants, using replacement dates and a spare-system recovery date as inputs. Directly optimizing the metamodel can select a poor strategy, so the authors introduce an adaptive search method called Quantile Function Expected Improvement (QFEI). In the VME study, QFEI found a strategy close to the best one in the tested search set with 50 additional simulator evaluations, although the assessment is limited to simulated data and a restricted candidate set.
narrate.key_results: For the toy problem, QFEI found the exact maximizing strategy in 22 of 30 trials; in the other 8 trials it found the reported near-optimal alternative. For the VME case, optimizing the median directly from the metamodel performed poorly: the true maximum was 0.82, while the metamodel maximum was 0.42, with a reported relative error of 5.4%. For the 40th quantile in the VME study, the best value in the search set was -1.72, compared with -1.95 in the initial design; after 50 QFEI iterations, the selected strategy had a value of -1.74. Across 50 repetitions with different initial designs, the selected strategy was always among the five best points in the tested set.

narrate.summary: The paper addresses estimation in survival analysis when unobserved differences between individuals affect their failure hazards, but the distribution of those differences is not known. It models the hazard as a Cox regression hazard multiplied by an unobserved frailty, and approximates the frailty distribution using a local mixture with relatively small variation. The authors estimate regression coefficients using a profile likelihood procedure and numerical optimization, and extend the method to an unspecified baseline hazard. They compare the method with an Expectation-Maximization method that assumes gamma frailty, using simulations and a clinical trial of recombinant human deoxyribonuclease (rhDNase) involving 645 patients with cystic fibrosis. In simulations with left-skewed frailty, the local mixture method has lower coefficient-estimation bias and variability than the gamma-frailty comparison method.
narrate.key_results: In 100 simulated samples of size 500 with left-skewed frailty, the local mixture method had bias and standard deviation of -0.0093 and 0.069 for the Beta(5, 1) case, compared with 0.038 and 0.082 for the Expectation-Maximization method. For the other left-skewed mixture, the corresponding results were -0.0016 and 0.068, compared with 0.048 and 0.079. In the gamma-frailty simulations with sample size 200 and variance 0.1, 0.2, and 0.4, the local mixture method had smaller standard deviation, while the Expectation-Maximization method had smaller bias. In the clinical trial, treatment-group coefficient estimates were nearly identical between methods: -0.039 and 0.061 for the Expectation-Maximization method, and -0.040 and 0.060 for the local mixture method; placebo-group estimates differed more.

key_equations.name: Frailty Cox hazard
key_equations.explanation: The hazard rate for individual i at time t equals that individual's frailty multiplied by the baseline hazard rate and the exponential of the individual's covariates times the regression coefficients.

narrate.limitations_stated: The method assumes that frailty contributes relatively small variation compared with the total variation. The authors also note that the boundary of the local-mixture parameter space may not be smooth in general; in such cases, singular points must be characterized or another optimization approach used.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The likelihood assumptions require frailty to be independent of the covariates and censoring to be independent and noninformative, which may not hold in many applied survival datasets. The empirical evaluation consists of simulations and one clinical-trial dataset, so the paper does not establish performance across other populations or failure mechanisms; it also gives no measured computation-time comparison.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors do not propose a specific future research plan. They state that nonsmooth boundaries in general local-mixture parameter spaces may require characterizing singular points or using other optimization approaches.
narrate.future_work_unstated: Future work could assess the method under informative censoring, dependence between frailty and covariates, and larger frailty variation, and could validate it on additional field or clinical datasets. It could also examine multiple failure mechanisms, time-varying covariates and operating conditions, and how coefficient estimates support system-level reliability or maintenance decisions.

narrate.summary: The paper introduces a flexible parametric lifetime model by combining a generalized Gompertz lifetime distribution with a power series distribution for a latent number of failure causes. The resulting model can represent increasing, decreasing, or bathtub-shaped failure rates and includes several familiar lifetime models as special cases. The authors derive distribution properties and present likelihood-based estimation using an EM algorithm and numerical methods. They assess estimation using simulated samples and fit the model and related distributions to glass-fiber strength measurements and phosphorus measurements from plant leaves. The proposed class fits both datasets, with its geometric form performing best among the compared models for the glass-fiber data.
narrate.key_results: In 1,000 simulated samples, the authors report convergence in all cases and state that average estimates are generally close to their true values; for a sample size of 100 with alpha 0.5 and theta 0.2, the average estimates were 0.491 for alpha, 0.977 for beta, 0.081 for gamma, and 0.212 for theta, compared with true beta 1 and gamma 0.1. For the glass-fiber data, the geometric GGPS model had the best fit among the compared distributions, with a maximized log-likelihood of -12.0529, a Kolmogorov-Smirnov statistic of 0.0993, a p-value of 0.5629, and an Akaike information criterion of 32.1059. For the 128-plant phosphorus dataset, the generalized Gompertz model had a lower Akaike information criterion (-388.2653) than the four-parameter alternatives, whose reported values were -386.3623 or -386.2653. narrate.summary: The paper introduces a bivariate lifetime distribution built by compounding a generalized linear failure rate (GLFR) model with a power-series distribution. The construction models two related lifetimes as maxima over a random number of bivariate observations, and it can represent dependence that includes probability mass where the two lifetimes are equal. The authors derive distributional properties and use an expectation-maximization (EM) algorithm to estimate parameters by maximum likelihood. They illustrate the method with paired scoring times from American Football League games played over three consecutive weekends in 1986. The authors report that the compound models fit the data better than the un-compounded bivariate GLFR model, though several fit criteria favor different models.
narrate.key_results: For the football scoring-time data, the bivariate GLFR-geometric model had the lowest Akaike information criterion (AIC), at -64.7250, narrowly ahead of the bivariate GLFR-logarithmic model at -64.7164; the un-compounded bivariate GLFR model had an AIC of -63.3400. In contrast, the un-compounded model had the lowest Bayesian information criterion (BIC), at -54.6517, compared with -54.2990 for the geometric model. The reported likelihood ratio test (LRT) statistics for the five compound models ranged from 149.6724 to 150.0651, with p-values of 0.0000 against the baseline model. The reported Kolmogorov-Smirnov (K-S) p-values were all above 0.0995 across the three evaluated variables, but the paper provides no separate estimation-accuracy or prediction-error assessment.

narrate.summary: This paper derives reliability expressions for coherent systems that can fail when a specified active component fails and are equipped with one general standby component. The standby begins in a cold state, switches to a warm state after a fixed time, and may be activated when the system fails; its condition after warm operation is represented through a virtual-age model. The authors consider perfect switching, switching that can fail, and a random warm-up period. Their results use independent, identically distributed active-component lifetimes and an independent standby lifetime, and are theoretical rather than estimated from lifetime data. A numerical illustration shows the reliability of one example system with and without standby protection, but the paper does not report numerical accuracy or quantified reliability gains.
narrate.key_results: The authors derive reliability formulas for general coherent systems using the system signature, and give a more explicit formula for a k-out-of-n system. They also show how imperfect switching changes the reliability contribution from the standby: it is multiplied by the probability that switching succeeds. For their three-component illustration, the system signature is (1/3, 2/3, 0); the plotted example uses exponential component distributions with rate 2, warm-environment and virtual-age functions equal to time divided by 2, and fixed switching times of 0 and 0.5. In that illustration, the plotted reliability with standby is higher than without standby, but no numerical improvement value is reported.

key_equations.explanation: R_imp(t) is reliability with imperfect switching at time t; R_perfect(t) is reliability with perfect switching; p is the probability that warm-to-active switching succeeds; and Pr(X_{n-k+1:n}>t) is the probability that the original active system survives to time t, with n the number of active components and k the required number.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors do not provide a formal limitations section. They note that the general expressions are complicated and illustrate their use with one example.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The derivations assume independent, identically distributed active-component lifetimes and an independent standby lifetime, so they do not address common-cause failures or dependence among components. The numerical illustration is not validation against field data, and the formulas rely on specified lifetime and virtual-age functions that may be difficult to establish for real operating conditions.
narrate.future_work_stated: None stated.
narrate.future_work_unstated: A useful next step would be to estimate the lifetime and virtual-age functions from field or accelerated-test data and validate the resulting reliability predictions in service. The analysis could also be extended to dependent failures, multiple standby units, additional failure mechanisms, and system-level cost or replacement decisions.

narrate.summary: The paper introduces the three-parameter Kumaraswamy inverse Weibull distribution for modeling lifetime and survival data. It is designed to represent increasing, decreasing, and unimodal failure-rate shapes, extending the inverse Weibull distribution. The authors derive distribution properties and describe both maximum likelihood estimation for censored observations and a Bayesian approach with independent gamma priors. They apply the Bayesian model to times for 69 Nelore bulls to reach 160 kilograms and compare its estimated survival curve with the Kaplan-Meier estimate. The plotted curves appear broadly similar, but the paper does not report a numerical measure of fit or prediction error.
narrate.key_results: For the 69-bull dataset, the reported posterior means are 6.656 for b, 177.5 for c, and 8.231 for beta. The reported 2.5% to 97.5% posterior intervals are 0.9829 to 29.76 for b, 154.9 to 227.5 for c, and 3.84 to 15.01 for beta. The Bayesian survival curve is compared visually with the Kaplan-Meier estimate, and the paper describes the model as performing very well; it provides no numerical accuracy or fit statistic for that comparison. narrate.summary: The paper introduces the Weibull Birnbaum-Saunders (WBS) distribution as a flexible extension of the Birnbaum-Saunders lifetime model. Unlike the original model, its failure rate can be decreasing, increasing, bathtub-shaped, upside-down bathtub-shaped, or modified bathtub-shaped. The authors derive distribution properties and estimate the model parameters by maximum likelihood. They apply it to two real datasets: failure and running times for 30 devices, and 40 turbocharger failure times. In both datasets, the proposed model fits better than the seven alternative distributions considered, according to the reported fit statistics.
narrate.key_results: For the 30-device dataset, the WBS model had the lowest reported negative twice the maximized log-likelihood, Akaike information criterion, Bayesian information criterion, consistent Akaike information criterion, and Kolmogorov-Smirnov statistic among the eight models; its Kolmogorov-Smirnov statistic was 0.1685 and its p-value was 0.3618. For the 40 turbocharger observations, it again had the lowest values of those fit criteria and a Kolmogorov-Smirnov statistic of 0.0778 with a p-value of 0.9685. In a simulation illustration, the authors compared the exact and empirical cumulative distributions using a generated sample of size 1000 and reported that the simulated values were consistent with the model. The paper reports parameter estimates and standard errors but does not report a prediction-error comparison.

narrate.summary: The paper proposes a model for residual lifetime when units have different, randomly varying ages. It forms a weighted average of the baseline unit’s residual lifetime distributions over the random ages. The model is intended for settings such as populations of used devices and components that remain alive after a system failure. The authors derive theoretical results about dependence, stochastic ordering, and aging properties, and illustrate the model with examples rather than lifetime data. They show that some aging properties are preserved by the model, while certain positive aging properties need not be preserved.
narrate.key_results: The authors prove that the model preserves decreasing likelihood ratio, decreasing failure rate, and increasing mean residual life properties of the baseline distribution. They also establish conditions under which stochastic orders between random ages carry over to the corresponding average residual lifetimes, and conditions for comparisons between models with different baseline distributions. For an exponential baseline, the random age and the modeled residual lifetime are independent. These are theoretical results; the paper reports no empirical estimation accuracy, prediction error, failure probability, or cost comparisons.

narrate.summary: The paper presents a Bayesian nonparametric method for estimating reliability in systems made from components arranged in series or parallel. Component or subsystem failure-time data, including right-censored observations, are used to build and update beta-Stacy process models, which are combined by matching their first two moments. The method can combine information from components, subsystems, and the full system, while avoiding Markov chain Monte Carlo for its main posterior calculations. It is evaluated using simulated aircraft-propulsion data and an industrial example involving a six-component product; the industrial data are obfuscated. In simulation, the method is less accurate than a correctly specified parametric model but more accurate and less biased than the misspecified parametric model, and the authors report substantially faster computation.
narrate.key_results: Across 30 simulated data sets, each with 30 observations from each component, subsystem, and full system and approximately 15% right censoring, the method's mean absolute error was 0.0311 and average bias was 0.0021. The correctly specified parametric model had mean absolute error 0.0179 and average bias 0.0048; the misspecified parametric model had mean absolute error 0.0391 and average bias 0.0280. The authors report that the nonparametric posterior took under 2 seconds, compared with about 45 minutes for 10,000 Markov chain Monte Carlo draws for the parametric models. In the industrial example, analysis of the six-component series system took approximately 1.88 seconds; its posterior mean lifetime was 716.7, median was 330.0, and 95th percentile was 2849.0.

narrate.limitations_stated: The model assumes that components are independent; violations can reduce accuracy. It does not handle interval-censored data, and the authors note that doing so would incur substantial computational cost because they know of no conjugate model for that data type.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The system-level process created by combining components is approximated as a beta-Stacy process by matching only its first two moments, so the approximation may not preserve other features of the system lifetime distribution. The industrial example does not provide direct validation on unmodified field data: the data are proprietary and disguised, and the analyzed component data were generated from fitted Weibull distributions.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors propose exploring copula models to account for dependence among components. They also propose extending the method to interval-censored reliability data, while noting the likely computational cost.
narrate.future_work_unstated: Further work could test the method on independently reported, unmodified field data and assess how well its uncertainty intervals are calibrated, especially in the lifetime tail. It could also incorporate operating conditions, component covariates, and distinct failure modes, then evaluate how those extensions support system-level reliability decisions.

narrate.summary: Sales dates for unreturned products are often unknown when manufacturers sell through retailers, so field failure records may omit both sales lag and lifetime. The paper models the joint distributions of sales lag and product lifetime while accounting for a warranty limit and the end of the observation period. It proposes a stochastic expectation-maximization method that imputes missing values and updates the distribution parameters. The method is evaluated using simulations and three real field datasets, including furnace, automobile-component, and telecommunications data. The authors find that it can estimate parameters in settings where direct likelihood maximization is unstable, while very high missing-data rates can still make lifetime estimates unreliable.
narrate.key_results: Across simulations with 5,000 replications, the proposed method estimated parameters for dependent and independent sales lag and lifetime models, and estimates were generally more accurate with longer warranty periods. In a comparison with Ghosh’s imputation method, the proposed method had smaller biases and root mean square errors in many tested settings and required less computation; for the furnace data it took 12.28 seconds, compared with 72.12 seconds for that method. With 2,000 units, direct maximization failed to converge when more than 80% of data were missing; at a 94.7% missing rate, increasing the batch size to 20,000 reduced the reported relative root mean square errors for the sales-lag rate, lifetime scale, and lifetime shape estimates from 32.2%, 26.1%, and 18.2% to 15.1%, 13.2%, and 6.0%. In the automobile example, 66 claims were observed among 589 units, and the fitted lognormal sales-lag and Weibull lifetime model had an Akaike information criterion of 1165.0. For the telecommunications data, 98.6% of units were missing and the lifetime parameter traces were unstable, which the authors interpret as possible evidence of insufficient information or estimation breakdown.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors report that when missingness is extremely high, such as 97% in their simulation, the root mean square error for a lifetime parameter becomes large and the method may break down. In the telecommunications example, the lifetime parameter traces were very unstable, suggesting large estimation bias or variance, insufficient information, or possible breakdown.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The core likelihood assumes that failures within warranty are reported without delay and that the units share the specified parametric model; departures from these assumptions could bias the estimates. Although the paper demonstrates the method on real datasets, the examples do not provide independent ground-truth parameter values against which to assess real-world estimation accuracy, and the telecommunications lifetime results show how weakly identified parameters can remain despite extensive computation.

narrate.summary: The paper addresses residual-life prediction when components degrade at different rates in different environments and their degradation records may be incomplete or observed only at sparse time points. It models each degradation path with basis functions and component-specific coefficients, while representing environments as discrete groups with different path distributions and measurement-error variances. An expectation-maximization procedure estimates the model, and the method predicts residual-life distributions for operating components from their partial measurements. The authors evaluate it using simulated signals and vibration measurements from rolling bearings tested at two rotational speeds. Accounting for environmental groups generally improves prediction over treating all components as one population, especially early in life, while classification and clustering give similar results in these studies.
narrate.key_results: In simulation, the estimated clustering had a Rand index of 1 for both complete and sparse signals, and the estimated group trends were close to the true trends. For complete signals at 10% of component life, the reported prediction-error result was 3.24 for both classification and clustering, compared with 4.58 without clustering; at 50% it was 0.21 versus 0.45. For sparse signals at 10%, the results were 6.18 for classification, 6.41 for clustering, and 7.52 without clustering; at 50%, they were 0.62, 0.64, and 1.33, respectively. In the bearing study, the 2600 rotations-per-minute group degraded faster than the 2200 rotations-per-minute group, and prediction-error medians and variances decreased as more of each bearing's lifetime was observed.

narrate.summary: The paper introduces the inverse Lindley distribution as a lifetime model intended for data with an upside-down bathtub-shaped failure rate. narrate.summary: The paper extends Bayesian estimation for a general failure-rate model in which the failure rate can represent several lifetime patterns. At those same settings, linex risk falls from 123.9033 to 36.62481, while entropy risk changes from 0.3094569 to 0.3146239. narrate.summary: The paper develops a step-stress accelerated degradation test in which all test units move to a higher stress level when a scheduled measurement shows that at least one unit has crossed a chosen degradation threshold. It models degradation with a gamma process and relates the process rate to stress using an Arrhenius relationship. The design jointly selects the threshold, number of units, measurement interval, and number of measurements to estimate a chosen lifetime quantile precisely within a cost budget. The authors illustrate the method using published carbon-film resistor information and use simulated data to examine the stability of parameter estimates. In their illustration, the optimal design uses 13 units, 52 time units between measurements, and 7 measurements for all considered quantiles.
narrate.key_results: For the carbon-film resistor illustration, the optimal design was 13 units, a measurement interval of 52 time units, and 7 measurements, with total experiment time of 1456 hours. For the median lifetime quantile, the optimal threshold was 0.0502 and the minimum coefficient of variation was 0.1300; the estimated median was 336650.3. Across probability levels from 0.1 to 0.9, estimated quantiles ranged from 292795.6 to 387073.5, and the minimum coefficient of variation declined from 0.1389 to 0.1218. A simulation with 10,000 iterations was used to assess parameter-estimate stability under selected designs, and the authors reported stability for small departures from the optimal plan.

narrate.summary: The paper addresses the mismatch that can arise when laboratory accelerated life test results do not predict field failures well. It models unobserved differences in field operating environments as a gamma-distributed frailty, linking a laboratory Weibull lifetime model to a field failure-time distribution. The authors develop joint likelihood-based inference using laboratory and warranty-return data, and optimize accelerated test plans to estimate field lifetime quantiles or warranty failure probabilities. They evaluate the methods with simulations and data from Appliance B, including laboratory tests and field warranty records. Their analysis finds that accounting for environmental heterogeneity can improve field fit and produce test plans different from plans that assume uniform operating conditions.
narrate.key_results: For Appliance B, the laboratory data comprised 10 tested units, with 8 observed failures; the field data covered 4,708 units and 93 wear failures. For field data, the Burr-XII model fit better than the Weibull model by the Akaike information criterion, with values of 1,953.5 and 1,958.4, respectively. The test of a common Weibull shape parameter gave a ratio estimate of 0.585 and a probability value of 0.217; the likelihood-ratio test gave a probability value of 0.244, and neither test rejected the gamma frailty model. In the simulation, for one reported setting, the proposed test's estimated Type I error was 0.057 at a nominal level of 0.05, compared with 0.072 for the likelihood-ratio test; for the stated field-quantile planning example, the optimal plan was (0.338, 0.649), with an asymptotic standard deviation of 3.23, versus (0.419, 0.766) when heterogeneity was ignored.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors state that the shape-parameter ratio test is exact under complete or Type II censored data, but only approximately pivotal under Type I censoring. narrate.summary: This paper develops a goodness-of-fit test of whether time-to-failure data follow an exponential distribution when some units are progressively removed from the test after failures. The method expresses the joint Rényi entropy of progressively Type-II censored failure times through a single integral involving the hazard function, then estimates that entropy from the observed data. The authors use the estimated entropy to construct a Rényi-Kullback-Leibler (R-KL) information test statistic and compare it with an existing Kullback-Leibler test. They evaluate the tests using simulated lifetime distributions with increasing, decreasing, and nonmonotone hazards, and illustrate the method with insulating-fluid breakdown data. In the reported simulations, the proposed test generally has higher power than the comparison test.
narrate.key_results: The authors estimated critical values and powers using 10,000 Monte Carlo simulations, and selected alpha equal to 0.4; the power comparisons use a 10% significance level. Across the reported simulation tables for sample sizes of 10, 20, and 30, the proposed test usually had greater power than the existing test against the tested Gamma, Weibull, Beta, and log-normal alternatives, though not in every individual comparison. For example, at sample size 20 with 10 observed failures and the scheme that removes 10 units after the first failure, the proposed and comparison tests had powers of 0.703 and 0.672 against the increasing-hazard Gamma alternative, and 0.231 and 0.039 against the decreasing-hazard Weibull alternative. For the insulating-fluid example, the proposed statistic was 0.2422 and the reported p-value was 0.9737, which the authors interpret as strong evidence consistent with exponentiality.

It could also extend the test to competing failure mechanisms and system-level reliability decisions, and compare the simulation cost with practical alternatives for obtaining critical values.

narrate.summary: Common-cause failures can make redundant systems less reliable, but data on joint failures are often sparse, and estimated failure rates can be very sensitive to prior choices, especially when some event counts are zero. The authors model uncertainty in the fractions of failures involving different numbers of components with sets of Dirichlet priors, and uncertainty in the total component failure rate with sets of Gamma priors. They combine these models to calculate lower and upper expectations for common-cause failure rates, using a Taylor approximation for the rate conversion and bounding its error. The paper illustrates the method with an example using 36 failure events for a four-component system and a separate fictional electrical network example. The method produces ranges rather than single estimates, allowing uncertainty about the analyst’s prior knowledge to be reflected in the results.
narrate.key_results: For the four-component example, the authors recommend an interval of 1 to 10 for the alpha-factor learning parameter; with 36 observations, the posterior expectation interval for the fraction of four-component failures is 0.00014 to 0.00109. In the fictional two-line network example, based on 11 observed events over 12 years per line, the estimated expected rate of double failures is 0.19 to 0.24 per year, and the rate of single failures is 0.318 to 0.373 per year. These are uncertainty bounds from the proposed approach, not results of a comparison against observed future failures or a competing method. The authors also report absolute approximation errors of 0.006 for the double-failure fraction and 0.003 for the single-failure fraction in this example.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors restrict the prior parameter sets to a particular convex form and note that other shapes might fit prior information or update better, but could be harder to elicit. They do not calculate imprecise credible intervals and expect that this would require an approximation procedure.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The model assumes exchangeable components, immediate repair, Poisson failures, and independence between the alpha factors and the marginal failure rate; these assumptions may not fit systems with unequal component health, delayed repair, or dependent failure processes. The network data are fictional and the method is not validated against field outcomes, so the reported bounds do not establish how well they predict operational failure rates.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors propose studying more general shapes for sets of Dirichlet and Gamma priors, including their elicitation and updating properties. They also identify the calculation of imprecise credible intervals as an unresolved issue that may need an approximation procedure.
narrate.future_work_unstated: A useful next step would be to test the approach on real utility or safety-system records and assess whether the reported bounds are calibrated against later failures. Further work could also relax exchangeability and independence assumptions by including component condition, operating conditions, and dependencies among failure mechanisms.

narrate.summary: The paper introduces the exponentiated Weibull-Poisson distribution, a four-parameter lifetime model intended to represent increasing, decreasing, bathtub-shaped, and unimodal failure rates. It models an observed lifetime as the maximum of a random number of independent exponentiated Weibull lifetimes, with that number following a zero-truncated Poisson distribution. The authors derive distribution and reliability properties and estimate parameters by maximum likelihood using an iterative latent-variable procedure. They apply the model to glass-fibre strength measurements and Kevlar 49/epoxy stress-rupture lifetimes, comparing its fits with exponentiated Weibull, generalized exponential, and Weibull distributions. The reported results support flexible fits, although model rankings differ depending on the fit criterion.
narrate.key_results: For the 63 glass-fibre strength observations, the proposed model had a Kolmogorov-Smirnov statistic of 0.1154 with p-value 0.3731, compared with 0.1901, 0.2291, and 0.1589 for the exponentiated Weibull, generalized exponential, and Weibull models. Its Anderson-Darling statistic was 0.682 and its Cramer-von Mises statistic was 0.195, both lower than those of the three comparators; its Akaike information criterion was 34.0, lower than the exponentiated Weibull and generalized exponential values but higher than the Weibull value of 34.4. For the Kevlar stress-rupture data, its Kolmogorov-Smirnov statistic was 0.0725, compared with 0.0844, 0.0887, and 0.0907 for those same comparators, and its Anderson-Darling and Cramer-von Mises statistics were also the lowest. However, its Akaike information criterion for the Kevlar data was 212.6, higher than the comparator values of 211.6, 209.6, and 210.0. For the glass-fibre data, the likelihood-ratio comparison with the exponentiated Weibull model gave a statistic of 3.4 and p-value 0.0651.

narrate.summary: The paper addresses early detection of cooling-system degradation in optronic equipment, where degradation can increase the equipment's cool-down time and may precede mechanical failure. It models operating condition as a hidden Markov process and uses a filter to estimate the probability of being in a degraded state from observed, smoothed cool-down-time measurements. The measurements come from operational logbooks for 28 appliances, with simulated data also used to examine the filtering method and its sensitivity to parameter choices. A maintenance rule sends an appliance for service when the estimated degraded-state probability equals one for three consecutive uses. In the operational data, the rule detected three of the five observed cooling-system failures before failure and raised no alerts for the 23 appliances without observed failure.
narrate.key_results: In simulations, the filter's estimated state probability tracked the known simulated state, and the authors report that the estimates were not strongly affected by the parameter deviations they tested. For the operational data, the selected rule detected three of the five appliances that failed before failure and missed two. It produced no detections among the 23 appliances without observed failure. The paper reports 26 good detections over 28 appliances, with no false detections.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors explain that the operational process generally stops at its first transition to degradation, so the long observation histories needed to estimate model parameters from repeated state transitions are unavailable. They therefore choose parameters using expert input and data from the appliances, and note that the twenty-startup moving average means the probability estimate cannot begin until twenty startups have occurred.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The operational evaluation uses only 28 appliances and five observed cooling-system failures, so performance estimates are uncertain and are not validated on a separate cohort. The method assumes a common model and independent appliance histories; moreover, overlapping moving averages can create dependence in the observations that is not represented by the stated observation-noise model.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors state that Thales is working to implement the maintenance algorithm in its health and usage monitoring system. They describe two implementation options: assessment by the equipment's embedded calculator or assessment by a maintenance laptop connected periodically.
narrate.future_work_unstated: Evaluate the rule prospectively on a larger, independent set of operational appliances, including more cooling-system failures, and assess how early alerts occur before failure. Extend the model to account for differences between appliances, operating conditions, and other failure mechanisms, and test whether maintenance decisions based on the estimated probabilities improve system-level availability and cost.

narrate.summary: The paper proposes a repair model for repairable systems whose failure rate decreases early in life, is then constant, and later increases. This pattern makes the usual definition of a perfect repair unsuitable, because returning a system to its new condition may not return it to its best-performing condition. The model represents repairs by changing the system’s virtual age, with the best condition placed at the first change point. The authors derive the resulting conditional failure intensity and illustrate it with a numerical example, not with observed system data. In that example, increasing repair effectiveness reduces the expected number of failures over the mission period.
narrate.key_results: In the numerical illustration, the expected number of failures over a mission time of 10 falls from 33.78 for a repair degree of 0 to 12.78 for a repair degree of 1. The expected count decreases as the repair degree rises, with the reported intermediate values also declining across the tested degrees. These are model-based calculations using the paper’s selected failure-rate parameters, not estimates from field or test data.

narrate.summary: The paper studies a dam whose water input is an inverse Gaussian process and whose release rate switches between zero and a fixed positive rate. Release starts when the water level reaches an upper threshold and stops when it falls to a lower threshold. The authors derive resolvent and first-passage results, then use them to formulate discounted cost, long-run average cost, and the stationary distribution of dam content. The analysis is theoretical and uses no data or numerical case study. The main finding is that the dam has a finite expected cycle length and an ergodic stationary content distribution only when the release capacity and input drift satisfy the stated stability condition.
narrate.key_results: The paper derives the transform of the time for the releasing dam content to reach the lower threshold and gives an expression for its transform parameter. It finds that the expected time to reach the lower threshold is finite only when M times mu is greater than 1; otherwise that time has infinite expectation. Under that same condition, the content process is ergodic and the paper provides a stationary distribution and a long-run average cost expression. No numerical accuracy, prediction-error, failure-probability, or cost comparison results are reported.

narrate.summary: The paper introduces the Kumaraswamy-Pareto (Kw-P) distribution by extending the Pareto lifetime model with two additional shape parameters. The added parameters broaden the possible distribution shapes and allow decreasing or upside-down bathtub failure rates. The authors derive distributional properties and estimate model parameters by maximum likelihood. They assess estimation in simulations and compare model fits using 72 flood-peak exceedances from the Wheaton River. The Kw-P model fits those data better than the Pareto, exponentiated Pareto, and beta-Pareto alternatives considered.
narrate.key_results: For the Wheaton River data, the Kw-P model had Akaike information criterion 548.4, Bayesian information criterion 555.3, and consistent Akaike information criterion 548.8, all lower than the corresponding values for the beta-Pareto, exponentiated Pareto, and Pareto models. Its Kolmogorov-Smirnov statistic was 0.1700, compared with 0.1747, 0.1987, and 0.3324, respectively. The reported negative twice log-likelihood was 542.4 for Kw-P, versus 567.4, 574.6, and 606.2 for those same alternatives. The simulation study used 1,000 replications at sample sizes 30, 50, and 100; the authors report that estimation bias decreased toward zero as sample size increased.

narrate.summary: The paper proposes a framework that combines Bayesian networks (BNs) with structural reliability methods (SRMs) to analyze engineering systems with both continuous and discrete uncertainties. It converts an enhanced Bayesian network (eBN) into a discrete-only reduced Bayesian network (rBN) by eliminating continuous nodes, using structural reliability calculations to obtain the probabilities needed in the reduced model. Exact inference can then be performed on the reduced network, including Bayesian updating when new evidence about discrete variables is available. The authors describe ways to reduce computational burden, including selective discretization, causal modeling, and combining parent variables into intermediate variables. The paper develops the method theoretically and uses conceptual examples; it does not analyze lifetime records or report empirical accuracy results.
narrate.key_results: The authors show that continuous-node elimination turns the required probability calculations into component or system structural reliability problems, after which existing exact inference methods for discrete networks can be used. They introduce Markov envelopes to identify which variables must be handled together; they advise limiting an envelope to about 15–20 discrete variables, even when each has only two states, because table and computation sizes grow rapidly. In a hierarchical example with five outputs and the same number of states per output, the original model requires the number of states to the fourth power times one less than that number of states in system reliability calculations; discretizing the shared continuous parent reduces this to five times one less than the number of states, or to one less when the components are identically defined. These are theoretical calculation-count comparisons, not measured accuracy or runtime results.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors state that the method can become computationally impractical when the model has large Markov envelopes, since the number of required calculations and the reduced network’s probability tables can grow rapidly. They identify the main limitation as difficulty representing complex dependence among discrete variables that is not characterized by causal relationships, such as a discretized random field.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The paper provides theoretical derivations and conceptual examples rather than a quantitative validation against field data or a benchmark showing actual accuracy and runtime. Its discretization approach can approximate dependence between continuous variables and their parents, and the alternative that separates children can underestimate dependence among those children.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors state that further work is required to address complex dependence structures among discrete variables that are not characterized by causal relationships; they note that principal component analysis has been explored as one possible route.
narrate.future_work_unstated: A useful next step would be to test the framework on field observations from infrastructure systems and quantify how discretization affects failure probabilities and evidence updating. Further studies could also examine changing operating conditions and system-level dependencies, and connect the resulting reliability estimates to inspection, repair, or emergency-response decisions.

narrate.summary: Equality observations such as measurements create a difficulty for structural reliability calculations because they have zero probability under continuous models, making the usual probability integrals unusable. The paper models such observations with likelihood functions and transforms each likelihood into an equivalent inequality by adding an auxiliary random variable. This lets standard reliability methods estimate failure probability conditional on the observations. The method is illustrated with a measured component capacity, a linear model with normal variables, and simulated fatigue crack growth with crack-depth measurements. The transformation is exact, and simulation can give an unbiased updated reliability estimate, while first- and second-order approximations can be inaccurate.
narrate.key_results: For the capacity measurement example, importance sampling gave a reliability index from 4.47 to 4.53, compared with the exact value of 4.49. In the linear and normal example, importance sampling gave 3.02 to 3.08, compared with the analytical value of 3.07. For the fatigue example, Monte Carlo simulation using 1 million samples agreed closely with the dynamic Bayesian network results; the second-order approximation substantially underestimated reliability and produced no results beyond 4 million stress cycles. The paper reports that the transformed formulation itself introduces no approximation and that Monte Carlo simulation provides an unbiased estimate with an error estimate.

narrate.limitations_unstated: The numerical demonstrations use constructed examples and simulated inputs, not validation against field measurements from an operating structure. The fatigue illustration assumes constant stress amplitudes, a geometry correction factor of one, and independent standard normal measurement errors, so its results may not transfer directly to more complex field conditions.

narrate.future_work_unstated: The method could be tested on field monitoring data and on fatigue cases with changing loads, more realistic crack geometry, and correlated or non-normal measurement errors. Further work could also connect updated component reliability to system-level decisions, inspection timing, and maintenance choices.

narrate.summary: This review explains how surrogate models can reduce the computational burden of estimating structural failure probabilities when each evaluation of the engineering model is expensive. Ordinary Monte Carlo simulation becomes inefficient for rare failures, while directly substituting a surrogate for the true limit-state function can produce biased estimates. The paper reviews polynomial response surfaces, polynomial chaos expansions, and kriging, including adaptive ways to select and refine them. It also describes an importance sampling method that uses a kriging surrogate to guide sampling and corrects its estimate using evaluations of the true model. Examples use computational outputs from a frame model and a simulated system reliability benchmark; the results show substantially fewer model evaluations in these illustrations.
narrate.key_results: For the frame example, the model has 21 correlated uncertain inputs and is evaluated at displacement thresholds from 4 to 9 centimeters. A sparse polynomial chaos expansion used 450 finite-element runs and estimated reliability indices with less than 5 percent error up to a reference index of 4; the reported errors across all thresholds ranged from 0.9 to 6.2 percent. narrate.summary: Rare properties are difficult to estimate with ordinary simulation because they are seldom observed, making the estimated probabilities imprecise. This paper presents a cross-entropy method that adjusts importance-sampling parameters for guarded commands in discrete-space Markov models. The parameters are optimized using weighted simulated paths, without explicitly constructing the full state space or transition matrix. The method is demonstrated on a simulated chemical reaction network and a repairable-system model. The authors report large reductions in estimated variance compared with ordinary Monte Carlo simulation, while noting that reliable error bounds remain difficult.
narrate.key_results: For the chemical model, the authors report an approximately 10^7 variance reduction for the property that the number of D molecules reaches at least 470, compared with the variance of ordinary Monte Carlo simulation. For the repair model, the reported variance reduction is more than 10^5. The repair-model probability estimate differed from the numerical result calculated by PRISM by -1.7%, using an average that excluded the first two estimates. The demonstrations used 1,000 simulations per iteration for the chemical model and 10,000 per iteration for the repair model; the reported variance reductions rely on sample variance as an indication of the true variance.

narrate.summary: Estimating very small failure probabilities with ordinary Monte Carlo simulation requires many system evaluations, especially in high-dimensional problems. It proposes guidance for tuning that sampler and choosing the conditional failure probability, and adds a Bayesian post-processor that gives a probability distribution for the estimated failure probability rather than only a point estimate. The authors illustrate the methods using simulated data for a linear reliability problem and a six-story steel frame subject to simulated earthquake ground motion. They find that the proposed tuning and level-selection rules perform well in their examples, and that the Bayesian output conveys uncertainty in the estimated failure probability.
narrate.key_results: For the Modified Metropolis algorithm, the authors recommend tuning its acceptance rate to between 30% and 50%; in two 1,000-dimensional examples, optimal scaling reduced the coefficient of variation of estimates for a failure probability of 10^-6 to about 80% of that with the reference spread of 1. They derive an approximately optimal conditional failure probability of 0.2 and report similar efficiency for values from 0.1 to 0.3. In the linear example with exact failure probability 10^-3, Subset Simulation estimated 1.057 × 10^-3; the Bayesian approximation had mean 1.064 × 10^-3 and coefficient of variation 0.16, compared with 0.28 for the frequentist estimate across 50 independent runs. For the structural example, the reference failure probability was estimated as 8.9 × 10^-3 using 4 × 10^4 Monte Carlo samples; Bayesian coefficient of variation decreased from 0.190 to 0.095 as samples per level increased from 500 to 2,000, while the corresponding frequentist values across 50 independent runs decreased from 0.303 to 0.131.

narrate.summary: The paper addresses the difficulty of predicting remaining life when degradation signals are observed sparsely or only during short intervals, rather than continuously from new to failed condition. narrate.summary: The paper addresses failure probabilities so rare that ordinary empirical counting may find few or no failures. It develops an estimator that uses generalized Pareto distribution (GPD) approximations for the two marginal tails and an extreme-value model for their dependence. The method expands a standardized failure set so that more observed extreme values contribute to estimating its probability. The authors analyze the estimator theoretically, construct confidence intervals, and study simulated data and Danish fire-insurance claims. They find that accuracy is often driven mainly by the estimation of the marginal tails, and that the proposed method can outperform an earlier estimator in their simulations.
narrate.key_results: In 1,000 simulated data sets of size 500, the target failure probabilities were generally between 0.0002 and 0.0005, making direct empirical estimates unreliable. For the Gumbel-copula example with Gumbel margins, the best results occurred with 50 to 150 upper-tail observations for marginal fitting and a blow-up product around 1,500,000; for reasonable choices, the earlier estimator's root mean squared error was usually at least twice as large. In the Danish claims example, based on 3,976 claims, the estimated conditional failure probability was about 0.00088, with a 95 percent confidence interval from 0.00022 to 0.00154; the event had occurred only twice in the observed period. narrate.summary: The paper addresses reliability data in which a manufacturer knows installation and failure times only for units that have failed by the end of the study. For the furnace data, the paper reports that truncated models without imputation greatly overestimated observed failures, while imputed models predicted better; the exponential-installation and Weibull-failure model performed best among those compared. narrate.summary: The paper introduces the G1-Renewal Process, a model for recurrent failures in repairable systems whose failure rate can increase or decrease over time. It changes the scale of each successive inter-failure-time distribution according to a restoration parameter, allowing it to represent improvement after repair as well as deterioration. The authors derive the cumulative intensity function and maximum likelihood estimation for exponential and Weibull underlying distributions. They use numerical illustrations, Monte Carlo calculations, and a published set of 12 consecutive failure intervals. The example shows that the model can fit a curved cumulative failure pattern even with an exponential underlying distribution, but the paper does not report comparative prediction accuracy.
narrate.key_results: For the example data of 12 consecutive failure intervals, the estimated exponential scale parameter is 4.781 and the estimated restoration parameter is 0.232. The fitted cumulative intensity function is convex, rather than the linear pattern that might be expected from an ordinary exponential renewal model. The numerical illustrations show that positive and negative restoration parameters can represent improving and deteriorating processes with exponential and Weibull underlying distributions. The paper reports no prediction-error, estimation-accuracy, or comparative cost results.

narrate.limitations_unstated: The real-data illustration uses only one published series of 12 failure intervals, and the paper reports no uncertainty intervals or comparison against alternative models. The analysis assumes independent inter-failure times and focuses on failure-terminated observations, so the paper does not establish how the method performs with right-censored observations or changing operating conditions.
narrate.future_work_stated: None stated.
narrate.future_work_unstated: Further work could assess parameter uncertainty and model performance on larger, independent operational data sets, including data with censoring and covariates such as load or environment. It could also test whether the model remains useful when repair effectiveness varies over time or when component failures interact at the system level.

narrate.summary: The paper studies degradation that is physically monotone but whose measurements may fluctuate or appear to improve because of noise or minor repairs. It models observed degradation as a gamma process plus an independent Brownian motion and estimates the model parameters using moments from degradation increments. The method is developed for independent items observed at potentially different, irregular times, with consistency and asymptotic normality established under stated sampling conditions. The authors evaluate it through simulations and two applications: a public National Institute of Standards and Technology dataset and heating-cable laboratory tests. Their results show improving estimates as the simulated sample size grows, while the heating-cable application has large parameter uncertainty and may fit poorly.
narrate.key_results: In simulations with parameters xi = 1, alpha = 0.02, and tau squared = 0.02, the reported empirical bias for xi decreased from 0.222 at 50 items to 0.0625 at 200 items; for alpha it decreased from 0.00555 to 0.00157, and for tau squared from 0.00621 to 0.000501. The study reports 1,000 repetitions and gives corresponding usable repetition counts of 937, 983, and 998 for sample sizes 50, 100, and 200. For the National Institute of Standards and Technology data at 65 degrees Celsius, the estimated tau squared was 0.0001, with a reported 95% confidence interval from 0 to 10.11; the authors say this result is consistent with a gamma-process model. For the heating-cable data, the 200 degrees Celsius estimate of tau squared was 0.03, with a 95% confidence interval from 0 to 2.81, and the authors note that large standard deviations make model choice difficult and may indicate poor fit; no competing-method comparison or reliability prediction is reported.

key_equations.name: Moment-based parameter estimates

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors report that the heating-cable data produce very large standard deviations, making it difficult to choose between the submodels and potentially indicating poor model fit. Under their stated results, consistency can be shown for one sampling case without establishing asymptotic normality, and neither property can be established for another case.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The model and asymptotic results rely on independent items and independent gamma-process and Brownian-motion components, as well as restrictive sampling conditions; the paper does not assess how violations affect estimates. Both real-data applications have only 15 items, and the reported intervals can be very wide, so the applications provide limited evidence about parameter stability or extrapolation to field conditions.
narrate.future_work_stated: The authors propose extending the model to include covariates, because the environment can influence degradation, and say this will be studied in a forthcoming paper.
narrate.future_work_unstated: Future work could test the method with larger field datasets and operating conditions beyond the laboratory examples, and assess how sensitive estimates are to the independence and sampling assumptions. It could also connect parameter estimates to failure-time or system-reliability predictions and maintenance decisions, which this paper does not develop.

narrate.summary: The paper addresses the difficulty of building a Bayesian network (BN) for degradation when experts cannot reliably provide the many conditional probabilities required by a complex model. It models a nuclear plant mechanical system using a BN whose complexity is reduced by representing it as a log-linear model and setting most higher-order associations to zero. The authors use expert judgments and, where available, operating feedback; they illustrate the method with a reactor coolant pump sub-component in French nuclear plants. They also describe rules for checking the consistency of elicited probabilities and working with experts to resolve inconsistencies. In the case study, the approach sharply reduced the number of probabilities needed, making the model more practical to populate and use for exploring maintenance actions.
narrate.key_results: For the 22-variable network, the required probability assessments fell from 381 to 69. For one node, the classical approach required 192 conditional probabilities, while the proposed approach required seven. The model included 17 binary variables and five variables with three modalities; after experts added nine conditional dependences, inference identified three environmental variables as influential in system degradation. The paper reports no estimation-accuracy or predictive-error comparison.

narrate.limitations_stated: The authors acknowledge that setting all associations above order two to zero may be too restrictive. They propose allowing experts to add selected higher-order associations when those are considered useful and reliable.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The probabilities depend heavily on expert judgments, while the authors say only a small amount of feedback experience was available; the paper does not provide an independent validation of the resulting probabilities against observed degradation outcomes. The conditional-independence assumptions may also omit important interactions, and the case study does not establish how well the model generalizes to other components or operating conditions.
narrate.future_work_stated: None stated.
narrate.future_work_unstated: A useful next step would be to validate the elicited probabilities and degradation inferences against a larger set of operational records, including data from other plants and operating conditions. Further work could also examine additional failure mechanisms and covariates, represent system-level dependencies, and test how maintenance decisions based on the network affect reliability in practice.

narrate.summary: This review describes statistical models for failure and maintenance events in repairable systems. It explains perfect, minimal, and imperfect repair models, including models that represent a system’s condition through virtual age, and develops the trend-renewal process as a way to represent both renewal behavior and time trends. It also discusses unobserved differences between systems, observed covariates, trend tests, and models for different types of events such as failures and preventive maintenance. The discussion draws on published operational and medical examples, including aircraft air-conditioner failures and engine valve-seat replacements. The paper emphasizes model structure and likelihood construction rather than a new estimator or a comparative performance study.
narrate.key_results: The review illustrates its models using Proschan’s data on 17 aircraft air-conditioner systems: the estimated between-system heterogeneity variance is approximately 0.11, and a likelihood-ratio comparison reports a statistic of 5.28, a p-value of 0.022, and an estimated trend power parameter of 1.16. For the Aalen and Husebye recurrent-event data, the renewal distribution is reported as non-exponential; the comparison of a renewal model with a trend-renewal model gives a likelihood-ratio statistic of 4.18, a p-value of 0.041, and an estimated trend power parameter of 1.14. The review also describes valve-seat replacement data from 41 diesel engines, where the estimated replacement frequency appears fairly constant up to 550 days and then increases. These are illustrative findings from the reviewed datasets, not a head-to-head evaluation of competing methods.

narrate.limitations_stated: The author restricts the discussion to operation time and assumes the system is restarted immediately after a failure or maintenance action, so repair durations and topics such as availability are not covered. The paper also gives limited attention to statistical inference and notes that nonparametric estimation can be challenging in some models. In the models for multiple event types, covariates and heterogeneity are set aside to simplify the presentation.
narrate.limitations_unstated: The examples are analyses of previously published datasets rather than prospective validation on new field data, and the review does not establish how well the models predict future failures or maintenance needs. Its demonstrations rely on assumptions such as independent, identically distributed systems in some analyses, while the breadth of the model families may make selection and estimation difficult for practitioners with sparse event histories.
narrate.future_work_stated: The author identifies challenging nonparametric estimation problems as an area needing attention. The paper also points to model checking and goodness-of-fit procedures as important tools when choosing among models.
narrate.future_work_unstated: Further work could validate these models prospectively on field data and test their predictions across changing loads, environments, and maintenance policies. It could also connect event-process models to system-level reliability and maintenance decisions, including the costs and effects of repair downtime.
